title: Mahershala Ali Says It ‘Doesn’t Matter’ That He’s Won 2 Oscars Because ‘There Are Not Roles for Me’ in ‘the Vast Majority of Projects’: ‘You’re Like Everybody Else Waiting’
description: Mahershala Ali got candid about the impact — or lack thereof — his two Oscar wins have had on his career in Hollywood while appearing on a recent e
body:
Mahershala Ali got candid about the impact — or lack thereof — his two Oscar wins have had on his career in Hollywood while appearing on a recent episode of Carmelo Anthony and Kazeem “Kaz” Famuyide’s “7PM in Brooklyn” podcast.

	The actor, who took home trophies for best supporting actor for both 2018’s “Greenbook” and 2016’s “Moonlight,” asked the hosts about the meaning of an Oscar, and if it really validates whether someone is “a good actor” or not. “There’s more good actors than there is good material,” he said. “It’s not even that all these people are competing for these same spots. It’s just that out of all the material made, there’s only a handful of them that check certain boxes.”
	

	He continued: “The vast majority of projects that get greenlit, there are not roles for me in those. You gotta think that way, you know what I mean? So, it doesn’t matter if I got 17 Oscars. If someone is not writing something for you or greenlighting something with you in mind, you’re like everybody else waiting and looking and searching.”

	While the star noted that actors could produce their own projects, the timeline is usually as least a “three to five year” journey. When asked by Famuyide if an Oscar win validates Black actors, Ali responded: “It’s kind of just talk. It doesn’t translate to anything real. You don’t want to find yourself in a situation where, oh, that’s ‘the diversity project.’ You just want to do great material as a Black person. You’re not thinking of yourself as this exotic other, per se. You just are living your life.”
	

	Most recently, Ali starred in Bassam Tariq’s “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” which hit theaters on Sept. 25. Tariq was also the original director of Marvel’s failed “Blade” movie, in which Ali was set to star in the title role, which he recently discussed in an interview with The New Arab.

	“It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script,” Tariq told interviewer Hanna Flint about his short-lived Marvel career. “You’re sitting there and explaining to actors what their role will be, and they just have to believe you. That’s also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn’t add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot. All I have is my integrity, and I’ve been thinking about that a lot.”

	“If you’re the bearer of bad news to your actors, but you’re not the one making any of these decisions — and it’s actually coming from a corporate entity — that’s not a great way to be a director,” he continued. “I know some people can take that and run with it, but I learned I was losing credibility with my actors, and it wasn’t a healthy way to operate as a filmmaker. Life’s too short to make shit films, so that was my big lesson: I have to have full control over my script. If we disagree, it’s between them and me. It’s quite sad because we had such high hopes for what we wanted to build.”

	Speaking of the film’s inability to get made, Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige had previously said he felt “like a gigantic loser and failure,” a statement that Ali agreed with in a GQ interview in the months following. “To this day, I don’t know why it didn’t happen. I just know that it was—Kevin, he said it was the biggest failure of his career and I agree,” said Ali.

schema.headline: Mahershala Ali Says It ‘Doesn’t Matter’ That He’s Won 2 Oscars Because ‘There Are Not Roles for Me’ in ‘the Vast Majority of Projects’: ‘You’re Like Everybody Else Waiting’

title: Seth Rogen Says Brad Pitt and ‘12 Years a Slave’ Cast Would Visit ‘This Is the End’ Set to ‘Perk Up’ Because They Were ‘in a Bummed-Out Headspace’ While Filming
description:
Seth Rogen and Brad Pitt spent time together while shooting very different films in 2013.

	Rogen recalled Pitt, Michael Fassbender, Chiwetel Ejiof
body:
Seth Rogen and Brad Pitt spent time together while shooting very different films in 2013.

	Rogen recalled Pitt, Michael Fassbender, Chiwetel Ejiofor and other cast members from “12 Years a Slave” spending time on the set of his comedy “This Is the End” while the two films were both shooting in New Orleans. In a recent appearance on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, he spoke about his friendship with Fassbender, with whom he starred in 2015’s “Steve Jobs.”
	

	“Actually, what’s so weird is I had met him — we made ‘This Is the End’ at the same time they made ’12 Years a Slave’ in New Orleans together,” Rogen told podcast host Josh Horowitz. “Understandably, the cast and crew of ’12 Years a Slave’ were in a bummed-out headspace a lot of the time.”

	“12 Years a Slave” starred Ejiofor as a free Black man named Solomon Northup who was kidnapped in 1841 and sold into slavery in Louisiana. Fassbender played plantation owner Edwin Epps and Pitt played an abolitionist named Samuel Bass who helped Northup regain his freedom.

	Meanwhile, Rogen was shooting “This Is the End” with Jay Baruchel, James Franco, Jonah Hill, Craig Robinson, Danny McBride and a host of other celebrities. The actors played dramatized versions of themselves in a bizarre apocalyptic scene at a Hollywood house party.

	“So they would come and hang out on our set, and we would go to bars and stuff, and they would come hang out with us all the time, I think just because we were in a great mood all the time,” Rogen said. “We were having the time of our lives, and then you’d see Steve McQueen and Brad Pitt and Chiwetel would sulk in, and then we’d give them a few drinks and they’d kinda perk up.”
	

	“12 Years a Slave” went on to win Best Picture and Best Adapted Screenplay (from Northup’s 1853 memoir “Twelve Years a Slave”) at the 2014 Academy Awards. Among its seven other nominations were acting nods for Ejiofor, Fassbender and Lupita Nyong’o.

schema.headline: Seth Rogen Says Brad Pitt and ‘12 Years a Slave’ Cast Would Visit ‘This Is the End’ Set to ‘Perk Up’ Because They Were ‘in a Bummed-Out Headspace’ While Filming

title: Stephan James on Honoring Carl Weathers’ Legacy and Learning to Box for ‘I Play Rocky’
description: Stephan James has played a few real-life figures in his career, including Olympic gold medalist Jesse Owens (in 2016’s “Race”) and civil rights lead
body:
Stephan James has played a few real-life figures in his career, including Olympic gold medalist Jesse Owens (in 2016’s “Race”) and civil rights leader John Lewis (2014’s “Selma”), so he knows the drill. Diving deep into the archives for research. Vocal coaching. Perhaps a physical transformation.

	His mission: honor the man, the mythic character he originated and their combined legacy. (Weathers died in 2024 at 76.)


	“It’s not lost on me, just how important Carl Weathers was not only in this franchise, but what he represented as a young Black leading man during that era,” James tells Variety, sitting down for an extensive interview about the role. “So, I just wanted to do that person justice and give him as many colors as I could in the short amount of time that I had in this film.”
	

	Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” now playing in theaters nationwide, focuses on the unbelievable true story of how Sylvester Stallone (portrayed by Anthony Ippolito) came to write “Rocky” and ultimately play the title role. But as much as the movie focuses on Stallone’s star-making moment, it also spotlights the key casting of Weathers, a former pro football star, who’d played bit parts on shows like “Good Times,” “The Six Million Dollar Man” and “Kung Fu.”

	James shines in the character’s introduction scene: a crackling sequence in which Weathers auditions to play Apollo Creed, the heavyweight champ whom Stallone’s underdog Rocky will fight. James’ Weathers struts in with his shirt unbuttoned to reveal impressively toned abs. When the casting director asks his age, he quips: “Honey, I’m young as the sun and old as spit. Whatever, you need me to be.” It’s all going swimmingly — he delivers his lines with panache; he’s got experience in the boxing ring (a fib, but we’ll get to that later) — until it’s time to read with a mumbling Stallone. 
	

	“Look, can we cut?” Weathers says, leaping to his feet to complain about his scene partner. “I would really do better if I had a real actor reading with me, goddamnit.” When he’s informed that Stallone is the writer and lead actor of the picture, he replies, slyly: “Well maybe he’ll get better.”



	The fine-tuned comedy is a different look for the 32-year-old Canadian star, best known for dramatic parts — like “If Beale Street Could Talk,” “Homecoming,” “The Piano Lesson” and “Ricky” — and he plays it all with a mischievous glint in his eye. 

	“He’s got so much presence. He’s so magnetic that it wasn’t hard,” James says about filming the sequence. “I just tried to step into the best version of myself, tap into all the presence and charm that I have — and it’s not as much as him — but, trying to take what was within me and just compounding on top of it.”



	

					Stephan James and Anthony Ippolito at the world premiere of “I Play Rocky” during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival; Sylvester Stallone and Carl Weathers in “Rocky.”
									2026 Getty Images / ©United Artists/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	While “I Play Rocky” coincides with the 50th anniversary of the original “Rocky,” the movie also comes after Creed’s legacy has been pushed to the forefront of the franchise thanks to Michael B. Jordan and Ryan Coogler’s blockbuster “Creed” trilogy. During the press run, James joked about calling up his “son” Jordan (as the Oscar winner’s Adonis Creed is the love child of the late boxing champ) to talk about the family business. 

	“I’ll tell you the truth: I did not call Mike, and we did not have this discussion,” James says, laughing. “But, I will say that I’m happy to be in the family.”

	To prepare for the role, James dropped between 20 and 25 pounds in two months and learned how to box for real. Read on for more about how he prepared for the part and the question he wishes he could’ve asked Weathers before production.
	
		One of the gags in the film is that Carl Weather claimed to know how to box, but he really didn’t. Is there anything on in the special skills section of resume that you’ve embellished?	

	The list is far too long for the 10 minutes that we have right now.
	
		Well, good news, we have 20.	

	Oh OK, cool. If I’m being honest, yeah, there are little white lies that you tell to help set yourself up for success. You don’t want to get caught in those lies too, though. So you want to make sure you can sort of deliver on it. Or that by the time they catch you in the lie, they love you so much that it doesn’t matter.
	
	
		When I talk to actors, the one that always seems to come up is they say they can ride a horse, and when they get on set, the producers find out they’ve never been near a horse.	

	Yep, I’ll say I ride a horse. I own a horse. I’ve even put that on my resume. So, you know, whatever you got to do.
	
		Wait, you actually own a horse? Or you just put it on your resume?	

	See, you believe me. That was good, right?
	
		I mean, why would you lie to me? To that point, what was the key to nailing Carl’s swagger in that audition scene?	

	More than anything, it was just fun. So many times when you’re performing, I’ll have moments where I’m like, ‘Oh, I can’t even be around anyone,’ or I’m so locked in and so hyper focused on lines, or trying to stay in a in a vibe or a mood. That wasn’t this [movie] for me. This was Peter Farrelly giving me the keys to the scene and being like, ‘Go do your thing.’ So, it was very rewarding to see how it finally turned out.
	
		Peter has said that he did not want to do this movie without you. That once he knew that you were a possibility to play the role, it needed to be you for this. How did this part come to you?	

	I just got a call from my manager, like most things, that they’re making this movie and that they were looking for Carl Weathers. And I was like, ‘Carl Weathers, yes. Where do I sign up?’ It didn’t take any convincing. I read the script. I was blown away by it. I put my tape together for Pete, and he liked it.
	
		What made you so quick to say yes? You’ve played Jesse Owens, John Lewis, so many of our real-life heroes, but it is always intimidating to step into someone’s shoes. So why were you like, “No, I cannot let this role pass me by.”	

	There’s an internal litmus test that a lot of actors have. Maybe they’ll admit it. Maybe they won’t. But a part of it is when you read something and you’re like, “I don’t want to see anyone else do this.” Like, “I feel like I have the most to add to it or bring to it, and I don’t want to see anybody else’s version of this. I want to do my version.” So, that was a big deciding factor. Just reading it and being like, “No, it’s too special” on the page; I want to be able to do it myself. These characters that mean so much, that are so impactful, it’s an honor. It’s like why wouldn’t I want to have that you know on my belt if you will, that I got to play Carl Weathers. It’s amazing!
	
	
		That’s a boxing championship belt in and of itself. What was one of the key stories that you read, listened to or got from someone that really helped you tap into Carl’s character?	

	His warmth was something that people don’t really get to see too much. Just looking at him, he could come across as like this physically imposing, maybe scary individual, but I’ve spoken to people who’ve spent a lot of real time with him, and you know they’ve all said just how kind he was.

	I tried to add that into the film just in terms of his relationship with Sly. When he finally admits that he’s not a boxer, and the fact that they could both laugh at that moment and then bond on something like, “Yes, we’re adversaries in this film, but, for the purposes of making this film, we’re gonna have to lock in and be able to trust each other, and it’d be nice if we liked each other too.”



	

					Anthony Ippolito (as Sylvester Stallone) and Stephen James (as Carl Weathers) in “I Play Rocky.”
									©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		You never got to meet Carl. What is one question you wish you could ask him?	

	I’d be keen to know if he really understood what he would mean to the legacy of this franchise, not only in the four “Rocky” films he made, but, if you count the “Creed” films [too]. The fact that there was a whole other world that spawned off people’s love for you and your character and your lineage, that we can make a whole series of movies about his son now.

	That really is Carl Weathers and his legacy. Not every actor rather is going to step into that role and last for four movies and then [influence] three more after that. Like, that’s because of him. So, I would wonder if he knew on those first days on “Rocky I,” like, did you ever think it could be this?
	
		That’s an incredible question because I can’t imagine that they did. This was all just a labor of love — a great story, a great script, great opportunity. And it’s turned into this massive, multi-generational franchise. You did do your own boxing training for this. What did your process look like?	

	I was just over 200 pounds when I found out that I got this job and I found out that I had two months to get ready for this. So, my initial thought process was, “Let me just start eating and bulking up,” like protein for breakfast, lunch and dinner, just go ham. And I spoke to a trainer friend of mine, and he said, if you work on cutting your body fat percentage down, effectively losing weight while keeping your muscle, you’ll be great. And people are gonna think you look bigger than you actually are. Trust me.
	

	So, that became my process: weight training at the gym in the morning; going down to Kingsway Boxing Club in Toronto with my trainer Jennifer Huggins and we just took it day by day, step by step. It started with cardio, just getting my endurance level up, then it was footwork. I didn’t realize how big footwork was in boxing. Just learning how to not move around like a baby deer. And then unlearning all of those things to be the unpolished version of Apollo Creed. There were layers and levels to it. By the time I was done, I ended up dropping like 20-25 pounds and in the film, I’m 170-175 max.
	
		How much fun did you have going toe to toe with Anthony recreating these epic boxing scenes?	

	I’m still healing from some of the punches I took, but it was a lot of fun to work with Anthony and spend so much time with him. Just getting close with him, building like a bond and a level of trust with each other. That’s crucial, time for character development. For us to actually be going through the motions of the choreography in that last fight scene, getting into the psychology of what it meant to be a boxer and respecting that art form, the process was equally as important as the filming itself.
	
		After this, you’re heading off to star in “Discretion,” a legal drama with Nicole Kidman and Elle Fanning. What have what have you enjoyed about going into that realm?	

	First of all, I wear like the greatest suits ever, so that’s really fly. They’re all like custom made, so hopefully the production will give them to me afterward, because like who else are they gonna fit? So that’s been really really cool.

	And then, just playing this young, smart, quick-witted lawyer has been really fun. I just feel like I’m stepping outside of myself and again giving the world something that they haven’t really seen me in.



	

					Anthony Ippolito (as Sylvester Stallone) and Stephen James (as Carl Weathers) in “I Play Rocky,” opposite Weathers and Stallone from “Rocky.”
									Courtesy Everett Collection / ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection

schema.headline: Stephan James on Honoring Carl Weathers’ Legacy and Learning to Box for ‘I Play Rocky’

title: Andrew Rannells Was Told to ‘Stay Away’ From Kevin Spacey After Meeting Backstage at ‘The Book of Mormon’; He Then Sent a ‘Handwritten Letter’ ‘Asking Me on a Date’
description:
Andrew Rannells recently revealed that Kevin Spacey asked him out while the “Girls” actor was starring in “The Book of Mormon” on Broadway.

	“I’ve
body:
Andrew Rannells recently revealed that Kevin Spacey asked him out while the “Girls” actor was starring in “The Book of Mormon” on Broadway.

	“I’ve never told this story before. He asked me on a date once,” Rannells said while guesting on “The Downside” podcast hosted by Gianmarco Soresi. “He sent me a letter to ‘The Book of Mormon.’ Handwritten.” The actors went on to explain that the Oscar winner came to see the musical and “came backstage” to meet him after the show.
	

	“There were always a lot of really fun people there, but sometimes they would bring them up into our dressing rooms, but with no notice,” he said. “So after the show, we’re getting changed. There’s a knock on my door. It was Goldie Hawn, Kevin Spacey, and Joel Schumacher. They were not together, but they all walked up together. So then we were all crammed in my dressing room.”

	Rannells continued: “Kevin Spacey was sort of rubbing my neck as we were standing there… Joel Schumacher, who was very close to me, he said, ‘Stay away from that man.’” That prompted Spacey to respond, “Hey! C’mon, c’mon,” he recalled. “And then like a week later, I got a handwritten letter from him asking me on a date.” Rannells concluded by noting he “never responded” to the note.

	Rannells originated the role of Elder Price in the long-running musical, performing from the show’s opening in 2011 through June 2012. The part earned him a Tony nomination for best leading actor in a musical. 

	Spacey’s sexual assault allegations came years later in 2017, when fellow Broadway actor Anthony Rapp said that the actor assaulted him in his New York apartment while Rapp was a teenager. Rapp later filed a $40 million civil lawsuit for sexual assault and battery in 2022, but a New York jury found Spacey not liable on all counts. Earlier this year, Spacey reached a settlement with three men who sued him over sexual assault claims, avoiding a civil trial in London that was set for October.

schema.headline: Andrew Rannells Was Told to ‘Stay Away’ From Kevin Spacey After Meeting Backstage at ‘The Book of Mormon’; He Then Sent a ‘Handwritten Letter’ ‘Asking Me on a Date’

title: Russell Crowe’s Request to Shoot ‘A Beautiful Mind’ Chronologically Added $1 Million to the Budget, Says Ron Howard: ‘It Was the Right Kind of Investment’
description: “A Beautiful Mind” director Ron Howard recently called Russell Crowe’s suggestion to shoot the film in order, which cost the studio an additional $
body:
“A Beautiful Mind” director Ron Howard recently called Russell Crowe’s suggestion to shoot the film in order, which cost the studio an additional $1 million, was “the right kind of investment.”

	The 2001 film follows mathematician John Forbes Nash Jr. (Crowe) through his academic career as he struggles with schizophrenia. Although many films shoot out of sequence, Crowe believed “A Beautiful Mind” would benefit from filming sequentially.
	

	“I am convinced it was the right kind of investment,” Howard told People magazine. “Russell certainly carried his part of the bargain with a brave and consistently detailed performance.”

	The director likened the approach to George Lucas’ on “American Graffiti,” where the “Star Wars” helmsman shot in sequence to highlight the “wear and tear” of night shoots on screen. Filming “A Beautiful Mind” in order could help Crowe develop a natural progression in his role.

	“Russell had, in passing, requested that we shoot the movie in sequence because the psychiatric journey and the way it would be revealed in the movie would be difficult to calibrate shooting the third act first and the first act second, which is typical for most movies,” Howard said.

	Shooting in sequence meant two separate trips to Princeton, N.J., adding about $1 million to production costs. But Howard stood by the approach.

	“I came to believe Russell was 100% right and had to dig in with the studio because it was about $1 million more to shoot in sequence,” Howard said.

	The sequential approach paid off. “A Beautiful Mind” went on to win four Oscars at the 2001 Academy Awards. The film took home best picture, alongside a best director win for Howard, best adapted screenplay and best supporting actress for Jennifer Connelly, who played Nash’s wife Alicia.
	

	A new 4K remastering of “A Beautiful Mind” hits theaters Sunday for its 25th anniversary.

schema.headline: Russell Crowe’s Request to Shoot ‘A Beautiful Mind’ Chronologically Added $1 Million to the Budget, Says Ron Howard: ‘It Was the Right Kind of Investment’

title: CAA’s Bryan Lourd Urges Congress to Pass NO FAKES Act to Combat AI Deepfakes: ‘Every One of Us Should Have the Right to Say No’
description: Creative Arts Agency CEO Bryan Lourd urged Congress on Saturday to pass the NO FAKES Act, a bill that would regulate the wave of unauthorized AI de
body:
Creative Arts Agency CEO Bryan Lourd urged Congress on Saturday to pass the NO FAKES Act, a bill that would regulate the wave of unauthorized AI deepfakes proliferating the internet, writing in a New York Times Opinion piece that “every one of us should have the right to say no to an unwelcome use of our likeness.”

	The NO FAKES Act was introduced by Sen. Chris Coons (D-ME) in May, following a previous attempt at the bill last year. While it advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in June and has a bipartisan coalition of co-sponsors, the full Senate has not taken it up. Lourd wrote that the bill would introduce a federal standard for “control, consent and compensation” surrounding deepfakes, replacing “outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind.”
	

	“I come to this issue not as a policymaker but as a practitioner. I run a global talent agency. Part of our job is to help our clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to AI companies,” he added. “We regularly negotiate those deals, and I can tell you that the bill pending in Congress delivers what the industry needs and what will protect all Americans.”

	Lourd laid out the stakes for Hollywood by citing Tom Hanks, who warned his followers in 2023 about a dental office using an AI deepfake of a younger version of him in an advertisement. Hanks likely wouldn’t have agreed to the dental ad, Lourd wrote, but he should’ve been given a choice before the dental office ran with an unauthorized deepfake.

	“What’s missing is a bright-line rule affirming that right in the AI age, and it is one Congress can supply before the year is out,” Lourd wrote.
	

	CAA has advocated against the unauthorized proliferation of celebrity deepfakes online, working with the Cate Blanchett-backed Human Consent Foundation to help people control permissions for their likenesses if they’re scraped by AI models. The agency also joined the foundation and other entertainment backers in an amicus brief in the New York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI, noting the active licensing market for likenesses that’s developed in the AI era.

	Deepfakes have been a constant presence since large-language models emerged in 2022, with many being used to produce unauthorized and sometimes explicit depictions of actors, singers and other celebrities. Other industry backers of the NO FAKES Act include SAG-AFTRA, the Motion Picture Association, the Recording Industry Association of America, the Recording Academy and the National Association of Broadcasters, OpenAI, the AFL-CIO, YouTube and IBM.

schema.headline: CAA’s Bryan Lourd Urges Congress to Pass NO FAKES Act to Combat AI Deepfakes: ‘Every One of Us Should Have the Right to Say No’

title: Jeff Goldblum Performs a Piano Medley and Reflects on His Career at Marrakech Film Festival: ‘The Stories That We Tell Matter’
description: Jeff Goldblum was honored with a tribute award at the Marrakech Film Festival on Saturday, delighting the audience with a surprise piano performanc
body:
Jeff Goldblum was honored with a tribute award at the Marrakech Film Festival on Saturday, delighting the audience with a surprise piano performance before reflecting on more than half a century in cinema, giving a heartfelt speech in which he thanked his many on-screen collaborators and insisted that “the stories that we tell matter.”

	The Hollywood legend was introduced by actress Tilda Swinton, who praised her “Grand Budapest Hotel” co-star as a “unicorn” and an “incomparable presence in cinema.”
	

	“I suggest that most of us would hesitate or demur these days in describing Jeff as an actor, because he is so very, very much more than that,” Swinton said. “Because what he shows us, always and seemingly forever, whether that’s representing anything and everything from a scientist, a grandmaster, a wizard, a fly, an alien, a consummate musician, an adoring father and husband, a friend, a comrade, is un-acted, un-pretended, Jeff. Open, warm, playful, sincere, kind, careful, understanding, interested.

	“Half a century of Jeff,” she added. “Hallelujah!”

	After a tribute video showcased iconic Goldblum performances across his career, including roles in “Invasion of the Body Snatchers,” “The Fly,” “Jurassic Park” and “Independence Day,” the curtain rose to reveal the actor — an accomplished pianist and jazz musician — seated behind a grand piano, from which he performed a medley of songs before a rapt crowd.

	Accepting the award after a lengthy standing ovation, Goldblum thanked the Marrakech Film Festival and “the people of Morocco, whose warmth is legendary,” before reflecting on the long journey that brought him to the stage in the Palais des Congrés.
	

	“When I consider the grand artists who have stood on this stage prior to me, I am infinitely humbled,” he said. “This award urges one to look back, and when I do, I don’t see a list of accomplishments. Certainly, I see faces, the people who gave me a chance before I even had earned one. I obviously didn’t get here by myself.”

	He went on to thank the many screenwriters, directors and actors who showed faith in him through the years before insisting that the work they do remains as vital as ever.

	“I believe that the stories that we tell matter,” the actor said. “At their best, films let us sit in the dark beside strangers and see the world through somebody else’s eyes. They remind us that we lucky creatures have an unfathomable measure of commonality, and they put to shame all those petty things which seem to divide us.

	“Movies also help us imagine something better — a world that works for everyone,” he continued. “That’s a planet toward which I want to keep working for as long as I have breath in my body, and with every story that I might still have the privilege to tell.”

	As well as Saturday’s honors, the Marrakech Film Festival is screening four films from the actor’s decades-spanning career: Lawrence Kasdan’s ’80s ensemble comedy-drama “The Big Chill,” David Cronenberg’s classic body horror “The Fly,” Roland Emmerich’s alien-invasion blockbuster “Independence Day” and Steven Spielberg’s “Jurassic Park,” the first installment in the dinosaur franchise juggernaut.

	The Marrakech Film Festival kicked off Friday night with a star-studded gala screening of Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” starring Oscar frontrunner Julianne Moore. Goldblum, who hammed it up on the red carpet outside the Palais alongside wife Emilie Goldblum, spent several minutes working the crowd, at one point stopping to autograph a hand-drawn portrait of the actor that was presented to him by a boisterous fan.

	Among the other celebrities in attendance were Swinton and Oscar winner and jury president Marion Cotillard, who heads a jury that includes “Sex Education” star Emma Mackey, “Phantom Thread” actress Vicky Krieps, “All of Us Strangers” filmmaker Andrew Haigh and “The Voice of Hind Rajab” director Kaouther Ben Hania.
	

	Also being honored with a tribute award this week are Moroccan actor Younès Mégri and American screen star John Turturro, whose most recent film, “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” will screen at the festival. He and Goldblum will both take part in the festival’s Conversation series, along with “Knives Out” director Rian Johnson, “Call Me by Your Name” Oscar nominee Luca Guadagnino, “Fjord” Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, Italian screen icon Monica Bellucci and more.

	The Marrakech Film Festival runs Nov. 20-28.

schema.headline: Jeff Goldblum Performs a Piano Medley and Reflects on His Career at Marrakech Film Festival: ‘The Stories That We Tell Matter’

title: How the ‘Elsinore’ Makeup Team Transformed Stars Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman to Bring the Story of Ian Charleson to Life
description:
In “Elsinore,” Andrew Scott plays real-life actor Ian Charleson, who performed his final role while dying of AIDS.

	Written by Stephen Beresford,
body:
In “Elsinore,” Andrew Scott plays real-life actor Ian Charleson, who performed his final role while dying of AIDS.

	Written by Stephen Beresford, “Elsinore” follows the deeply emotional and inspirational true story of Charleson as he confronts his mortality with courage, honesty and wit. On Nov. 13, 1989, Charleson walked onto the stage at London’s National Theatre to play Hamlet for the last time. He was dying of AIDS, a fact he kept secret. Very few of the 1,000 audience members at the Olivier Theatre knew his story.
	

	The biopic (currently in theaters) reunites Scott with Olivia Colman, who previously starred alongside him in “Fleabag.” This time, their bond is a special one as Colman plays Margaret Johnson, the doctor who treats Charleson.

	For “Elsinore,” both actors needed to transform themselves — not only into the real people they were portraying, but also back to the 1980s. That’s where makeup department head Nadia Stacey played a key role. Stacey, who was honored at last month’s Middleburg Film Festival, spoke about her work and approach to the film, explaining that “when there are real people, you have to be sympathetic to them.”

	Stacey described the ’80s as a tricky period to recreate, given it can easily become clichéd. “You immediately imagine everybody had a perm,” she said. “My approach every time is that you shouldn’t notice hair and makeup unless you actually want to notice hair and makeup. The story told itself. I just needed to tell his journey and put us in the era we were in without overdoing it.”
	

	Stacey worked to achieve a look that embodied Scott’s portrayal of Charleson while keeping everything authentic. “We know Andrew as that — jet black hair and brown eyes,” Stacey explained. Charleson, however, had blonde hair and blue eyes. “We didn’t want to push something too far to jar the audience. Andrew and I talked about it, and we said we should approach it in the sense of how an actor at that time would have done it. They would have been dyeing their hair themselves.” Instead of bleaching Scott’s hair, Stacey gave him a full head of blonde highlights and blue contact lenses, capturing Charleson’s defining characteristics.

	She would also track his journey after Charleson tested positive for HIV in 1986. As Charleson’s health declined, Stacey discolored Scott’s skin tone and added dark circles. For the sarcoma lesions, she used tattoo transfers, which she applied to Scott’s body.



	

									Anthony Dickenson
	



	Joining Stacey for the conversation was Colman, who also underwent a transformation to play Johnson. “The second you put a wig on someone, as an audience, you know they’re wearing a wig. So it’s hard to make sure that it looks good,” Stacey said. “I felt like we were telling a story about real people, and we needed to be as close to that as possible without pulling her out of the story. But from all the photos we had of Margaret, we know she had this blonde bob, so we tried it.” And it worked.

	Colman had also done her research on playing Johnson and knew how important it was to stay as close to the character as possible. She recalled, “We tried on the wig in the makeup room, and because I had been watching Margaret, I was very much up for a wig.”



	

									Anthony Dickenson
	



	Colman pointed out that the film doesn’t glorify Charleson’s death. Throughout the film, casting director Jessica Ronane cast background actors who actually knew him. David Rintoul — Charleson’s actual best friend — plays the Ghost of Hamlet’s father. Some of the hospital cast were also friends of the late actor.

	Colman shared, “The most interesting thing about finding out about Ian is every single person he spoke to said, ‘Ian was hilarious. Ian was funny.’ And so they wanted that. Everybody that they approached said, ‘Absolutely. Yes, please, count me in.’”
	

	In the film’s final act, Johnson comes to see Charleson. The camera focuses primarily on Johnson being moved by his performance. “Andrew, bless his heart, came to be there that day. It was only on me, and they’d already filmed the other bits, but he insisted. On a very long, exhausting shoot, on his day off, he came in and said, ‘Absolutely, I’ll do it for you.’ So he was performing bits of ‘Hamlet’ for me.”

	Fast forward to the film’s premiere at the London Film Festival, and Colman reflected, “I cried as it started till the end and had to pass tissues to the person next to me as well. And I think, for me, even though I’d seen it, it was seeing him in it and what it took to do that. He’s so incredible and so generous and so fun. Honestly, if I could just choose a handful of people to work for the rest of my career, he would absolutely be one of them.”

	Colman also shared the film’s powerful response: “There’s something beautiful about film reminding you of these past heroes.”

schema.headline: How the ‘Elsinore’ Makeup Team Transformed Stars Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman to Bring the Story of Ian Charleson to Life

title: Celluloid Sounds: Fewer Women Composers on Screen, But Some Hit the Right Notes
description: The stats for women composers in Hollywood have not improved. Just eight of this year’s top 100 grossing films feature original scores by women; th
body:
The stats for women composers in Hollywood have not improved. Just eight of this year’s top 100 grossing films feature original scores by women; the past two years have seen percentages between 7 and 9%, all down from 14% in 2023.

	But female composers continue to be in the awards conversation, and not all for their music. Laura Karpman, composer of “American Fiction” and the current Netflix miniseries “East of Eden,” has entered her first film as director in the documentary short subject category: “Cosmic Symphony.”
	

	The film is a timely look at four musical artists who lost priceless, beloved instruments in the Palisades and Eaton fires of January 2025: composer Starr Parodi, whose 1928 Steinway piano was heard in dozens of MGM scores including “The Wizard of Oz”; songwriter Diane Warren, who lost a Yamaha grand; jazz bassist John Clayton, whose string bass was nearly 200 years old; and Altadena educator Susie Chung, whose brown Steinway was played by Lady Gaga in “A Star Is Born” and on the 2019 Oscarcast.

	“I believe my piano has a soul… I have a little regret that I left her alone,” Chung says in the film, and that sentiment is echoed by the other musicians. “Instruments have hearts, they have souls, they have lives,” says Warren, a 17-time best song nominee. Two days before the fires, Warren was filmed performing her Oscar-nominated song “The Journey” on the piano in her Malibu beach house.

	Clayton’s bass, once owned by the legendary Ray Brown, had accompanied Ella Fitzgerald, Frank Sinatra, Nat King Cole and Duke Ellington. Recalling its past, he said “that bass and the music that it made was bigger than any of us could ever be.”
	

	Parodi describes her lost keyboard as having “this beautiful, haunting, bell-like sound… warm and thick,” and she tells the harrowing story of watching her house go up in flames via their doorbell camera and later unearthing the remains of her MGM piano in the rubble.

	Thousands of instruments were reduced to ash during the L.A. fires. “I felt it was a story that was really important to be told,” Karpman says. “When you live with these instruments, they have personalities, they see history.”

	In addition to the interviews and performance footage, she added lively, colorful animation to the story. Animator Tempe Hale sought “to make the instruments come alive again, (to convey) the kind of fun and glory and energy that these instruments have.”

	Karpman also composed the score for her film, incorporating both orchestral and choral sounds to suggest the music still being made, in the beyond, by those lost music makers.

	Scottish composer Anna Meredith wrote one of the year’s most unusual scores for the romantic fantasy “Wicker,” which stars Olivia Colman as a fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her artificial husband, made for her by a basket weaver in their medieval village.

	The entire score is played by just four people: a violist, a cellist, a recorder player and Meredith herself. “I’d much rather start small with a tiny lens, and see what you can do with it, rather than have every sound in the world, where it could just sound like any old thing. You have to really think creatively,” she says.

	Directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson reached out to Meredith during shooting (to write music for a wedding scene), and she quickly became part of a team that included several women in key roles (including editor Sofi Marshall). The composer decided that the timeframe and the nature of the story demanded wooden instruments for a “timeless quality.”

	Meredith used as many as 10 different recorders, “from tiny little baby ones, only 20 centimeters; lots of ones in the conventional treble tenor range; and some bonkers instruments, including a bass one and a contrabass one which was so tall we had to move to a different recording studio. We had to find one with a skylight to fit the neck of that one, like seven feet tall.”
	

	The recorders represented the fisherwoman and her wicker husband, while the strings (the darker sounds of viola and cello) represented the villagers. “It’s not nice string sounds,” she says, “it’s slithery, nasty sounds. Their sound worlds are, initially, kept quite different, and then the strings sort of ‘infect’ the recorders as the villagers start to impose on their relationship.”

	The directors “wanted the score to be bold,” Meredith adds, “and it’s loud as well. The music is upfront. I’m very proud to be part of a film with a strong female story and so many important female elements, both on and off the screen, that have been part of it.”

	For “Tenzing,” the untold story of the Nepalese-Indian Sherpa who accompanied Edmund Hillary to the top of Mount Everest in 1953, Norwegian-born, Stockholm-based composer Rebekka Karijord insisted on cultural authenticity. “I felt, early on, that we needed to have a collaboration with Nepalese musicians that isn’t like an exotic tone or a color,” she says. “It had to be a deep collaboration.”

	She enlisted a Nepalese spiritual leader and Buddhist nun, Ani Choying Drolma, to contribute traditional Buddhist chants; Nepal’s premier flautist and throat singer Manose Singh; and actress Thinley Lhamo, who plays Tenzing’s wife Dawa in the film and is also a highly regarded singer of Tibetan opera.

	Lhamo “has the most amazing voice,” Karijord says. That voice becomes, in a sense, the sound of the mountain itself. “I wanted to have something that could transcend the physical effort, that could pull us into the spiritual aspect, and her voice really solved that for me throughout the score.”

	In addition, she had the sound team record a number of unique sounds from the region—yak bells, goat bells, the sound of prayer wheels in the temples, Tibetan singing bowls and gongs—which she and her percussionist sampled and added to her musical library for incorporation into the score.

	The film details England’s drive to be the first nation to reach the summit of the world’s tallest peak, Karijord points out. “It needed the big cinematic muscles, a meeting between Western and Eastern. If I could make the mountain, this goddess, beautiful and pristine and dangerous and magnetizing, then we will understand why’re drawn to her—both Tenzing as a little boy growing up at the foot of the mountain, and these Englishmen wanting to conquer it.”
	

	Karijord employed a 40-piece string section from the London Contemporary Orchestra, in part to convey the danger of crevasses, avalanches and rumbles in the ice, along with a handful of woodwind and brass players and a 12-voice choir. Textural elements, such as the sound of breathing, also became a factor in the score.

	Regarding the few female composers scoring studio films, Karijord notes that “it’s such a deeply empathetic craft to score films, and it’s a deeply collaborative craft. I know a lot of women who are both very empathetic and collaborative and brave. So I think there should be more of us doing it.”

	Actor Awards Predictions: Andrew Garfield, Inde Navarrette and ‘The Odyssey’ Lead an Unsettled Film Race as ‘Widow’s Bay’ and HBO Max Could Rule TV
	



			
			
	
						

									Neon
	
					


							
		

	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change based on buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.



	

					OBSESSION, Inde Navarrette
									©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection
	




	2027 Actor Awards Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: Nov. 21, 2026): Seven. That’s how many nominations “The Odyssey” is projected to collect, which would tie the all-time record for a film at the Actor Awards, going back to the SAG Awards days. That record is only a year old, when “One Battle After Another” earned a record-breaking seven nods last season. Christopher Nolan’s epic is projected to land: cast ensemble, stunt ensemble, Matt Damon in lead and four supporting slots split between John Leguizamo, Robert Pattinson, Anne Hathaway and Samantha Morton.

	Andrew Garfield’s turn as Sam Altman is the early favorite for “Artificial” that could bring him his first trophy. Breakout Inde Navarrette would be the season’s most unlikely lead actress nominee and maybe its most deserved with her possessed girlfriend in “Obsession” carrying a microbudget horror film to the top of Focus Features’ box office history. If there’s any place that can truly challenge Julianne Moore’s remarkable turn in “The Debut,” it’s here.

	And noteworthy reminder, Amanda Seyfried is not eligible here for “You Can See Everything.”

	On the TV side, HBO Max takes 13 of the 45 projected slots and “The Pitt” returns as the reigning drama ensemble champ. Last season, Noah Wyle made history by winning all five major acting awards in one season for his role as Dr. Robby, and he could do it again. But the most-nominated series isn’t predicted to be the medical drama. It’s “Widow’s Bay,” Apple TV’s comedy, with five: ensemble, stunts, O’Flynn and a potential head-to-head in lead comedy between Matthew Rhys and Stephen Root. That matches the total from last year, when “The Studio” led TV with 5 noms. “DTF St. Louis” and “The Diplomat” follow with three each, and the drama actress race may be the one to watch. Keri Russell, who earned the honor for Best Actress in a Drama Series for “The Diplomat” last year, is back in the lineup, but she’ll have to fight off newcomer Emmy Rossum (“Furious”) to take her title.

              A California teen was pulled out of a car engulfed in flames just in the nick of time after a train collision ... as harrowing bodycam footage shows officers working hard to yank him from the fiery wreckage.
      
    
              It all went down on Nov. 18 in the San Bernardino area ... as Colton Police officers responded to an Amtrak collision with a Mercedes-Benz.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The Colton PD wrote ... "Upon arrival, officers encountered an overturned vehicle engulfed in flames with the driver trapped inside. Officers quickly worked to remove the driver from the burning vehicle and bring him to safety before rendering medical aid."
      

              Thanks to their quick actions ... the 18-year-old driver survived ... NBC Los Angeles reported.
      
    
              In the dramatic clip ... one officer can be seen pulling over to the scene of the crash before reaching into the inferno and pulling out the teenage driver, dragging him to safety.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The cause of the collision remains under investigation.
      
    
              As for the driver, they were transported to a local hospital. The Colton PD added ... "Our thoughts are with the driver as he recovers."
